newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds end softer, ignore U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds end softer, ignore U.S. data.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed slightly softer on Friday after a quiet week as investors ignored non-inflationary U.S. February producer prices amid continued fears the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike interest rates.

Canada's 30-year benchmark bond dipped C$0.13 to C$109.50 to yield 7.188 percent against the U.S. 30-year benchmark, which rose 4/32 to yield 6.95 percent. The spread between the two widened to 24 basis points from 23 at the close of trading on Thursday.
Analysts said North American bond markets have been driven by extremely strong U.S. retail numbers released on Thursday.

On Thursday U.S. government said February retail sales jumped 0.8 percent, compared to economists' forecasts of a 0.6 percent gain. Also, the January sales gain was revised upward to 1.5 percent from a 0.6 percent gain.

Investors are increasingly expecting the U.S. central bank will raise short-term interest rates to quell burgeoning inflation. However, the Bank of Canada is seen keeping Canadian rates steady to spur the sluggish economy, UBS Securities Vice President Pierre Bergeron said.
"Quite clearly the Bank of Canada has room to stay put," Bergeron said.

In other news NAV Canada, the newly privatized national air traffic authority, priced two bonds totalling C$750 million. It issued a C$500 million 7.56 percent bond due 2027 to yield 7.564 percent and a C$250 million 6.45 percent bond due 2004 to yield 6.459 percent.

In other prices, the Government of Canada's 7.00 percent bond due 2006 rose C$0.05 to C$103.35 yielding 6.526 percent while the U.S. 10-year rose 2/32 to yield 6.69 percent. The negative spread narrowed to 16 basis points from 17.
The three-month cash T-bill yielded 3.03 percent against its U.S. equivalent which yielded 5.24 percent.
